item.title: Another Crab's Treasure
item.description: A crab’s life should be easy: you go into your shell, protect yourself from the birds and live your life. There on your shore, without anything to worry about. What the hell is a job? What the hell are taxes? What even is the massive construct of society that oppresses us, that makes us always be productive in the name of money, which we call Capitalism? That’s what Kril, the protagonist of this game, would tell you before starting their story. This is the game created by Aggro Crab studio, a small indie studio located in Seattle, which a lot of you may know because of another game they developed afterwards, called PEAK. It follows the story of a hermit crab that sees their life change from one moment to the next, because of unpaid taxes, taxes that started some tides ago because some duchess said so. But Kril, not familiarized with the concept of taxes, has no money (trash) to pay these taxes, and the IRS (Shark Stick? I do not know what to call it) embargoes Kril’s shell. From that moment on, their mission is only one: recover their shell. As you, my attentive reader, may have noticed, the currency in this world is trash, more specifically, for us players, microplastics. The sea, polluted by humans, and the sea-life (crabs, hermits and others) transform the economy to be dependent on trash: you have to work for trash, you have to have trash; if you have no trash you belong to the low layers of society, if you have a lot, you are an elite. But this has consequences, as we know, trash and pollution are dangerous for us (humans) but also for sea life like the ones that belong to this story. And that produces gunk, which transforms the citizens of the sea into brainwashed, crazy, murderous beings.

item.title: Mixtape
item.description: There are a lot of games out there: games that make you feel happy, others sad, others that make you wonder why the fuck you are even playing that. Others are only entertaining, others you forget in less than a month, and others stay in your mind for a long time. But independent of that, the reason they stay in your mind is because they did something that connected with you, and because they were what they intended to be and showed you that. There is a phrase about writing critiques of any piece of art that has stayed in my mind since the first time I read it. You should judge art for what it is trying to be, not for what you think it should be. With that in mind, I will judge it without knowing the intentions of the developers. For games, at least, that seems the better way to critique them, because you, the reader, will not know them either. You do not care that the developers are some dudes from Australia called Beethoven & Dinosaur, or that the publisher is Annapurna Interactive, or that the director is Johnny Galvatron. Or do you?

item.title: Everdeep Aurora
item.description: Everdeep Aurora is a game. A great game? No. A bad game? Neither. Would I recommend it to a friend, a colleague, or a game aficionado? Probably. It wouldn’t be the first on the list, but I could. When I was deciding what rating to give, on the meaningless scale of 1-10, I could not decide. This is not a game that I hate, it’s not frustrating, it’s not badly made, and it’s not full of bugs or any of those problems. But at the same time, I could not tell you anything the game excels at.

item.title: World of Goo 2
item.description:
Introduction

World of Goo 2 is a sequel to the 2008 game with the same name, it is a game solely about putting balls into a hole. Let me rephrase, it’s a game where you create a structure to reach a pipe at the end that will suck your balls. Ok, that’s not better… Let’s try again, you have balls, pipes, sucking and fluids and you… Ok, jokes aside. The game is created by the same studio 2D Boy and now with the help of Tomorrow Corporation, which is basically another studio with the same indie developers as the first one, or almost the same. You can even see the same art style from the World of Goo series in the Tomorrow Corporation games that include great titles like Human Resource Machine and 7 Billion Humans that are both also puzzle games but less physics and more programming-like puzzles.

item.title: Control
item.description:
Control is a game developed by Remedy Entertainment, a Finnish studio. The creators present a unique atmosphere that should be praised in terms of creativity, going away from the typical fantasy, mythology, or on the other end, the sci-fi that we are so used to. For that, they venture into the realm of the paranormal, but not the folklore kind. Instead, one set inside a brutalist, capitalist office building.

The story begins with Jesse Faden, who is looking for her brother Dylan. That search leads her to enter the FBC (Federal Bureau of Control), a secret agency that works to hide from public view any kind of paranormal activity, with the help of her inner dialogue guiding the player through the world. These paranormal activities are called AWEs (Altered World Events), that can happen anywhere, alongside other concepts we will not mention to avoid spoilers. The game comes with its own terminology, which makes it more believable in the sense that this is a governmental agency that has everything categorized, defined, and buried in its own bureaucracy. And with bureaucracy, normally, comes hierarchy, which this agency also has. In the first minutes of the game, you find that the Director is dead (Trench), and by taking his weapon you become the new one, chosen by the Board. The Board is an unknown entity whose only shape and form we see is an inverted pyramid. And this is the setup, which, at least for me, is quite appealing.
